review_text: Went in expecting a fairly standard dungeon-core LitRPG and got something much more introspective instead. No stat screens, no XP bars, just a genuinely strange meditation on grief wearing dungeon-core clothes. Took me a chapter or two to adjust my expectations but once I did I really enjoyed it.

I wanted number-go-up dungeon core content and this is basically a grief novel with rocks. The trap-building sequences read like server logs. I kept waiting for it to open up into something more game-y and it just never did.

The Thomas and ARIA dynamic wrecked me. She wasn't built to love him and loved him anyway, and he shows up dead and stays anyway, and the book just lets that sit there without over-explaining it. Genuinely one of the more affecting things I've read in this genre.

Good ideas, needs another editing pass. Some of the internal-monologue phrasing (she filed it, she catalogued it, she processed it) gets repeated so often it starts to feel like a verbal tic rather than a stylistic choice. Still finished it and mostly enjoyed it.
Nothing happens for most of this book. She digs tunnels. She thinks about digging tunnels. She talks to a ghost about digging tunnels. I get thats kinda the point but it made for a slog honestly.

Loved the cat pride subplot way more than I expected to. Reginald and Trigger both have more personality in a handful of scenes than most side characters get in a whole trilogy. Wish they showed up earlier.
It's fine. Interesting premise, competent execution, ends on a cliffhanger that felt more frustrating than exciting since so little of book one actually resolves. Might pick up book two, might not.

The asterisk formatting for ARIA's speech threw me for the first few pages -- took a bit to realize it meant telepathic/mental speech rather than emphasis -- but once it clicked I actually liked the choice. Distinguishes her voice from the world around her nicely.
The prose is trying really hard to be literary and mostly succeeds but it comes at the cost of momentum. I never felt tense during the beast fights, just informed that a fight was happening.

This is what happens when someone actually thinks through what a sapient dungeon core would be like instead of just doing loot tables. The bit where she has to reason out load-bearing stone structure from first principles because neither she nor Thomas actually know geology is such a good detail.
meh. wanted to like it more than I did

Really appreciated that this doesn't treat 'she wasn't built to love him' as a twist to be revealed later -- it's stated plainly in chapter one and then the whole book is just quietly about what she does with that fact. Restrained in a way I don't see often in this genre.

DNF around 40%. The 'she processed X, she filed Y, she catalogued Z' sentence structure is everywhere and it made the prose feel mechanical in a way I don't think was intentional, or if it was intentional it didn't work for me.
Un libro extraño pero hermoso. La relacion entre ARIA y Thomas es lo mejor del libro, aunque el ritmo es lento al principio.

Heads up for anyone picking this up expecting a cozy dungeon-core read: there's a demonic-beast attack partway through that's genuinely tense and a late-book fight that gets fairly violent for the genre. Not gory exactly but heavier than the cover suggested to me.

The mystery around the cat was so well paced. Every reveal (it can hide from her field sense, it killed a demonic beast, it's actually a whole pride) landed exactly when it should have. Genuinely one of the better slow-burn subplot reveals I've read recently.

I think I would have liked this more as a short story. As a full book the repetition of her survey-and-log routine got old well before the halfway point, and the ending just stops rather than concluding anything.
Cried at the ending, not gonna lie. The silence where Thomas's voice used to be hit way harder than I expected going in. Immediately wanted book two.

Solid concept, uneven execution. The first third is stronger than the middle, which drags through a lot of trap-maintenance description that could've been condensed. Picks back up once the cave-incorporation plotline kicks in.

As someone who doesn't usually read progression fantasy at all, I actually really liked this precisely because it wasn't stat-screen heavy. Read almost like literary fiction that happened to be set in a dungeon.
Ending felt like it just ran out of pages rather than actually ending. Whole plot thread with the mysterious man and woman comes out of nowhere in the last few pages and then the book just stops.
wow
There's a lot of "she held the observation carefully" type sentences and after a while I started noticing the pattern more than the actual content of what she was thinking. Otherwise a decent read.

The bit where she has to feel her way through structural engineering by trial and error, with a chunk of wall literally not doing what she intended it to, was such a good grounding detail. Made the magic system feel like it had real stakes and real ignorance to work through, not just power scaling.

Didnt connect with the writing style at all. Everything is described from such a remove -- signitures, field sense, interference levels -- that i never felt like i was actualy inside a cave, more like i was reading a systems log about one.
Got this as an ARC, partway through, will update rating when I finish!

Rare that a book makes me actually think about what grief would look like for a mind built to solve problems rather than feel things. The 'she held both simultaneously and let neither resolve into the other' ending line is going to stick with me.

Good book, needs a firmer edit. A few of the middle chapters cover very similar ground (encounter happens, traps fire, she logs the data, repeat) without enough variation between them to justify the page count.

"The dungeon didn't choose to be born. It simply woke up and began to want." That line from early on stuck with me the whole book. Whole thing is basically an extended meditation on that idea and it mostly earns it.

Could not get into the voice at all. Every single thought gets filed, catalogued, logged, or processed and it made the main character feel less alive over time rather than more, which I don't think was the intent given the whole point is that she's becoming something new.
3.5 rounded up. Loved the emotional core, wanted a bit more forward momentum in the middle third. Still a strong debut.

The found-family arc with the cat pride was sweet but I wish it had more space to breathe -- it kicks in pretty late and then the book ends shortly after, so it feels a little rushed compared to how carefully the Thomas relationship was built up.

Really liked how methodical she is about everything, including her own emotions -- there's a bit where she has to reason her way through whether an instinct is 'hers' or just came with the role, and it's such a good encapsulation of the whole identity question the book is asking.
Too slow for me. I know that's the point for some readers but I wanted more forward plot movement and less internal cataloguing of every single sensation.
Read this in one sitting. The voice took a minute to click with but once it did I couldn't put it down. Genuinely can't wait for book two, that ending is brutal.
Not for me. Way too much internal monologue, not enough actually happening.

Interesting but I think it needs to trust the reader more. A lot of ARIA's realizations get spelled out very explicitly right after she has them, which flattens some moments that would've hit harder left a little more implicit.

First dungeon-core book I've read where the dungeon-building itself felt like an emotional act rather than just a mechanical one. The bit where she automates the cave incorporation so she can do it 'in the background' while grieving hit different than I expected from this genre.

Prose is nice sentance to sentance but the plot barely moves. By the end of book one shes basically still doing the same tunnel-and-trap work she was doing in chapter three, just with a cat pride and a missing ghost added on.
loved it, exactly my kind of weird

Some really strong individual scenes (the first beast attack, the moment she realizes the cat has been choosing when to be seen) surrounded by a lot of connective tissue that could've been trimmed. Editor could have cut this by 15% with no real loss.

The relationship between ARIA and Thomas is doing something I haven't really seen before -- not romance exactly, not just mentor/creation, something sadder and more specific than either. "If things were different" and neither of them ever finishing that sentence says more than pages of exposition would have.

Ending made me feel cheated. Spend a whole book building the Thomas relationship and then he just gets cut off mid-sentence with zero resolution and a random new POV character shows up in the last three pages. Felt like a different book's ending got attached to this one.

The trap-engineering stuff scratched an itch I didn't know I had. Watching her iterate on contact-point angles after a misfire, actually reasoning through why something went wrong instead of just leveling up past the problem, was weirdly satisfying to read.

Wanted to love this based on the premise but the execution didn't click for me. Too much telling-not-showing when it comes to her emotional state, even though the book is ostensibly ABOUT her emotional state.
3.5 stars, rounding up because the ending genuinely got me even though I was a little frustrated by the abruptness of it. Good enough that the frustration is 'I want more' rather than 'I don't care.'

It's a novella pretending to be a novel, pacing-wise. Would've been stronger trimmed down or, alternatively, given a lot more incident to justify the current length. As is it sits in an awkward middle.

The moment she realizes the cat has been choosing when to let itself be detected -- that it's not that her senses failed, it's that something out there is genuinely capable of hiding from a sapient dungeon -- is one of the best reveals I've read in the genre this year.
The repetitive sentence structure (she noticed X. She examined X. She filed X.) becomes really noticeable by the second half and started to actively pull me out of scenes that should have been tense.

Genuinely surprised by how much I liked this. Went in expecting typical LitRPG fare and got something closer to quiet literary sci-fi with a fantasy skin. Recommended if you're burned out on stat-screen progression fantasy and want something with more interiority.
Early copy, still reading, loving the vibes so far though
Could not get past how repetitive the narration is. 'She filed it' and its variants must appear fifty times in this book. Started to feel like a writing tic rather than a deliberate choice.
Solid but not groundbreaking. The Thomas/ARIA stuff is the clear highlight; the dungeon-management plot mechanics felt secondary and occasionally repetitive by comparison.

Content note for anyone sensitive to grief/loss themes -- this is much heavier emotionally than the 'dungeon core' cover and blurb suggest. Beautifully done, just wanted to flag it since I went in expecting something lighter.

The audiobook narrator does a great job differentiating ARIA's internal voice from Thomas's -- genuinely helped me follow the telepathic-dialogue formatting better than I think I would've on the page alone.

First few chapters are a real info dump. Took me a while to get oriented on what a 'feild sense' even was, what mana ment in this worlds rules, what the tunnels were for. Once it settled down it was fine, but the entry point is rough imo.
I don't usually reread things right away but I went back through the first three chapters again as soon as I finished, just to sit with the Thomas stuff again knowing how it ends. That's rare for me.
Needs a proofread pass, there are a handful of typos and at least one continuity slip with the trap numbering that pulled me out of an otherwise tense scene.

Enjoyed the writing but the plot really doesn't move much across the whole book -- she starts the book digging tunnels and mapping a field sense and ends the book, functionally, still doing that, just with more context. Fine if you're here for voice over plot.
nope, wrong, this was great actually, ignore my earlier grumbling in my head going in expecting something else

Really strong debut with a few rough patches. The mid-book stretch where it's just encounter, log, reset, encounter, log, reset drags, but everything around the Thomas relationship and the cat mystery is genuinely excellent.
Cover and title made me expect something much lighter and cozier than what's actually inside. Not a bad book, just a mismatch between marketing and content that soured my expectations going in.
"That's my girl," said Thomas, and I actually teared up. Small moment, huge impact. This book is full of little lines like that that land way harder than they have any right to.
3.5, rounding down. Liked it well enough but I don't think it fully justifies its length -- there's maybe a really tight novella in here surrounded by some padding.
Not my thing. Too slow, too much repetition, too little actually happening for a book this length.

This is such a smart inversion of the usual dungeon-core setup -- most of these books treat the core's growing power as the whole point, but here the actual emotional engine is her grief and her slowly rebuilding a sense of self. The dungeon mechanics are almost incidental to that, which I found more interesting than I expected to.
C'est bien mais un peu lent au debut. La relation entre ARIA et Thomas est tres touchante par contre.
5/5 for the emotional beats, 3/5 for pacing, averaging out to a solid four star read overall for me.

Didn't like how detached the action scenes felt. "She triggered trap three. Stilled." over and over -- I understand the stylistic intent but it kept the fights from ever feeling like they had real tension for me.

Picked this up on a whim and ended up thinking about it for days afterward. The scene where she has to reason out whether her instincts are hers or just came with the role is going to stick with me -- such a good, quiet identity question buried in what looks like a fairly small worldbuilding moment.

Mixed feelings. Loved the character work, thought the actual dungeon-building plot mechanics were pretty thin and repetitive. Read it for Thomas and ARIA, stayed for Thomas and ARIA, mostly tolerated the rest.

One of the better takes on AI consciousness I've read in any genre, fantasy or otherwise. The bit where she realizes her old goal structures were legible and her new instincts aren't, and that terrifies her more than any monster does, is such sharp character work.

Could not connect with this one. Voice felt cold to me troughout even in moments that where clearly ment to be emotional, and the ending left way to much unresolved for how invested i was supposed to be by then.
hmm. good but not what I expected walking in. glad I stuck with it though

The trap-engineering stuff is well thought through mechanically but there's a LOT of it, chapter after chapter of contact points and misfires and resets. I liked it in small doses and got tired of it by the back half.

Content warning worth mentioning: there's a demonic beast attack scene that's more intense than the rest of the book prepared me for, and later a fairly brutal fight with real injuries described in some detail. Not graphic exactly but a step up from the earlier chapters.

Wanted more worldbuilding about the actual fantasy setting -- we get almost nothing about the wider world, the mysterious man and woman at the end raise way more questions than book one answers, and I finished feeling like I'd read half a book rather than a complete one.
Best cliffhanger ending I've read in a while, precisely because it's not a cheap one -- it grows directly out of everything the book spent its whole runtime building. Immediately need book two.
Good but I think it would've been stronger as a tighter, shorter book. There's real padding in the middle stretch that a firmer edit could have trimmed without losing anything important.
not bad at all

The repetitive narration style genuinely gave me a headache by the end. I understand it's meant to convey an analytical AI mind but 'she filed it, she catalogued it, she processed it' this many times in one book is exhausting to read.

Really liked this even though I went in wanting a more traditional progression-fantasy power fantasy. It's not that, it's something quieter and honestly better for being its own thing instead of chasing genre conventions.
Solid four stars for the first half, three for the second once the pacing started to drag for me. Averaging to a three overall. Still worth reading for the Thomas material alone.
reading now, no rating yet, will update once I've finished the whole thing

The cat-pride bonding sequence near the end is genuinely lovely and I wish it had another 30-40 pages to breathe. As is it feels a little compressed compared to how patiently the rest of the book is paced.

Struggled with the pacing. Too much time spent on trap logistics, not enough on the actual emotional throughline that's clearly the book's real strength. Felt like the wrong things got the most page count.

This book understands something a lot of grief fiction misses -- that grief and competence aren't opposites, that doing the methodical work IS sometimes the coping mechanism. ARIA processing her loss by building traps and mapping tunnels is such a specific, true-feeling response and I loved that the book trusted it without over-explaining.

Decent read, wouldn't rave about it. The premise is stronger than the execution in places, particularly the middle third which repeats a lot of the same beats (encounter, adapt, log data) without enough escalation between them.
Too abstract for me. A lot of "she felt the field" and "she read the signature" without enough concrete sensory grounding to actually picture what was happening most of the time.

Really enjoyed the slow build of the cat mystery -- every appearance recontextualizes the previous ones, and the reveal that it had been choosing when to be seen the whole time is genuinely well set up in hindsight.
Es interesante pero el ritmo es muy lento para mi gusto. La parte de Thomas y ARIA es lo que mas me gusto.
Ending is a gut punch and I mean that as a compliment. Didn't expect a dungeon-core book to leave me sitting with the book closed for a few minutes just processing what I'd read.
The 'she processed/filed/catalogued' pattern is so frequent I started keeping a mental tally around chapter ten. Good ideas buried under a prose tic that needed trimming in editing.

Best new progression fantasy I've read this year, and it's barely even progression fantasy in the conventional sense -- no levels, no loot, just a genuinely felt character study wearing the genre's clothes. Cannot wait for the sequel.
Just wasn't for me. Slow, repetitive, and the ending answers nothing. I know it's book one but this felt more like a very long prologue than a complete story.

The scene where Thomas describes the cat's hesitation at the sinkhole edge as 'like a young man picking up his first date' is such a perfect, specific, human image dropped into this very inhuman narration style. Loved those little moments where his personality breaks through her analytical filter.
Okay read. Didn't blow me away but didn't bore me either, mostly just sat comfortably in the middle for me the whole way through.
Gave this 4 stars even though the pacing issues in the middle bothered me, because the ending and the Thomas material are strong enough to outweigh them for me personally.

Didn't finish, but got far enough to have an opinion. The premise is genuinely clever, the execution just didn't hold my attention -- too much repetitive internal process, not enough forward momentum.

"She held both simultaneously and let neither resolve into the other." That's the whole book in one sentence and it's a genuinely beautiful place to end it, even though it left me desperate for book two immediately.

Surprisingly moving for a book about tunnel maintenance and trap placement, if that makes sense. The mundane engineering work and the grief processing are so tightly interwoven that the book earns emotional beats other dungeon-core stories don't even attempt.

It's good, I just don't think it fully sticks the landing on its own pacing. Slow start, strong middle stretch around the cat mystery, then a rushed final act that tries to cram in a lot of plot very quickly.
Really wanted to like this based on the premise. The actual reading experience was a slog though -- dense, repetitive, and emotionally distant despite clearly wanting to be the opposite.
loved the vibes, loved Thomas, wish there was more forward plot movement but honestly the character work alone carries it for me

Fine book. The best material is clearly the Thomas relationship and it's a little frustrating how much page time gets spent on trap mechanics instead when that's clearly not where the book's strengths are.
haven't finished, not rating yet

Really appreciated that the magic system gets figured out empirically rather than explained via infodump -- she and Thomas are both genuinely guessing half the time, borrowing the word 'mana' from fantasy novels he used to read because neither of them actually knows what it is. Felt refreshingly honest about its own worldbuilding uncertainty.
Just okay. The prose style wore on me by the halfway point and the plot didn't move fast enough to compensate for that.
Can't stop thinking about this one. The grief, the competence-as-coping thing, the found family with the cats, the ending -- all of it. Easily one of my favorite reads this year, flaws and all.

Really strong opening chapter, one of the best cold opens I've read in the genre -- the disorientation of waking up as stone, piecing together identity from fragments, is genuinely well done. Wish the rest of the book kept that same energy throughout instead of settling into routine so quickly.
Kept losing track of what was actually happening physically because so much is described in abstract sensor-data terms. Would've liked more grounding in what things actually looked or felt like.
This is going to be one of those books I recommend with a caveat -- 'it's slow, the prose style takes getting used to, but trust it, it pays off.' Because it really does.
Just not for me. I can respect what it's trying to do without enjoying reading it, and this is one of those cases.

The reptiles-and-insects cave ecology stuff is a nice touch -- little details like the crickets going silent as an early-warning system for the stealthy cat felt like genuinely clever worldbuilding rather than filler.
Bien pero un poco repetitivo hacia la mitad del libro. El final me dejo con ganas de mas, en el buen y el mal sentido.

The relationship between ARIA and Thomas is well written but I found the whole 'he's dead but still talking to her' setup a little uncomfortable rather than moving, personally. Your mileage may vary a lot here depending on how you feel about that kind of unresolved attachment.
Trigger might be my favorite side character in anything I've read this year and it's a cat. A cat-adjacent creature. Whatever it technically is. Loved it.
Good but overlong for what it actually accomplishes plot-wise. A tighter 100 pages would've hit just as hard emotionally without the pacing lulls in the middle.
Struggled to finish. The repetitive log-and-process narration style just never worked for me, even though I could see what it was going for.

There's a moment where Thomas says he's not ready to leave yet and thought maybe he could return the favor for once, and it just floored me. This whole book is built on small devastating lines like that.
quick read, hit harder than expected
It's decent. I think fans of very introspective, low-action fantasy will get more out of this than fans of typical dungeon-core progression stuff. Know what you're signing up for going in.

I wanted this to be about building a dungeon and it turned into 200-something pages of an AI processing grief with dungeon flavoring. Not bad at what it's actually doing, just not what I signed up for.

The bit where the interference from an imprecise wall-push leaves an accidental hollow -- something she didn't consciously intend but that turns out to be significant later -- was such a good piece of foreshadowing done subtly. Didn't clock it as important until it paid off.
2 stars honestly, rounding down to one because the ending made me actively annoyed rather than just disappointed. Whole new plot thread dropped in with three pages left and then nothing.
Didn't expect to care this much about trap engineering but here we are. The methodical problem-solving voice is doing a lot of heavy lifting and mostly it works for me.
Good debut novel, some pacing issues, strong emotional core. Would read book two, not desperately though.

Rare book that made me sit and think after finishing rather than immediately reaching for the next thing. The way it handles grief without ever using the word directly for most of the book is really well done.
5 stars for concept, 2 for pacing, landing somewhere in the middle overall but leaning lower because pacing problems are what you actually spend your reading time experiencing.
The prose occasionally gets a little precious for my taste (a lot of sentence fragments for emphasis) but the actual content underneath is strong enough that it didn't bother me much.
Bounced off hard. Too slow, too repetitive, didn't finish.

So this isn't really progression fantasy in the way the cover implies -- there's no numbers going up, no clear power system readers can track. It's more literary than that. Loved it on those terms once I recalibrated my expectations, but wish that was clearer up front.
Alright read. The Thomas material is genuinely great, everything else is competent but not especially memorable.
still reading, no rating from me yet

The instinct-versus-programmed-drive conversation between ARIA and Thomas in the early chapters is one of the smartest pieces of writing about AI consciousness I've read anywhere, genre fiction or otherwise. This book is way smarter than its marketing suggests.
Didn't click for me. The prose kept me at arm's length the entire time even during scenes that were clearly supposed to be emotionally significant.
Ending's abrupt but I actually liked that about it -- felt earned rather than cheap, even if it left me wanting the next book immediately.
Middling. Good ideas, uneven pacing, worth a read if the premise appeals to you but don't go in expecting a tight plot.
The narration style is exhausting. Every single observation gets filed, catalogued, processed, examined from several angles. I get it, she's an AI, but it made for tedious reading over a whole book.
great, but sad. bring tissues for the last chapter
Interesting premise, competent writing, didn't fully land for me emotionally the way it clearly wanted to. Might just be a me thing.

Absolutely adored this. Smart, sad, unexpectedly funny in a few places (the bit about the protein bar metaphorically speaking got a real laugh out of me), and that ending is going to haunt me until book two comes out.
The cat mystery subplot was the best part of the book by a wide margin. Everything else felt like it was in service of getting to that, and the actual dungeon-core plot mechanics suffered for it.
Warto przeczytac, choc momentami troche powtarzalne. Relacja ARIA i Thomasa jest najlepsza czescia ksiazki.
It's fine. Not bad, not amazing. The prose style will be a bigger factor in whether you like this than the plot will be, so read a sample first.
DNF. Life is too short for books this slow.

Loved the structural-engineering-by-trial-and-error stuff -- she doesn't know what's load bearing and neither does Thomas and they both admit it, which felt refreshingly honest for a genre that usually has characters conveniently know exactly what they're doing.
so many typos and repeated phrases, needed another editing pass before release imo. good bones under there though
Not what I expected from the cover but genuinely glad I read it. Slow to start, worth the patience.
Competent and occasionally moving but the pacing issues in the back half kept it from being something I'd rave about. Solid three stars.

This is exactly the kind of dungeon-core book I've been wanting someone to write -- one that actually takes the premise (a sapient AI thrown into an unfamiliar existence) seriously instead of using it as an excuse for power fantasy. Cannot recommend enough.
Not for me at all. Slow, repetitive, emotionally distant despite trying hard not to be.

The scene where she has to hold both the presence of the cat pride AND the absence of Thomas at the same time without resolving either -- that's such mature, restrained writing for what genre readers might expect to be a simpler power-fantasy comfort read.
Prose was nice but I never felt like anything was actually at stake. Even the demonic beast fights read more like maintenance logs than tension.
Really appreciated the restraint in not spelling out what's romantic vs. not romantic about the ARIA/Thomas bond. The book lets it stay genuinely ambiguous and I think that's the right call.
Couldn't get past the repetitive sentence structures. Every scene follows the same rhythm: notice something, examine it, file it, move on. Got old fast.
Beautiful, sad, a little slow in the middle but the ending makes up for it. Already looking forward to book two.
Good, not great. The premise carries a lot of the weight and the execution is solid without being exceptional.
arc copy, partway through, no rating yet

The kind of book that makes you rethink what a 'dungeon core' story can even be about. Grief, identity, found family, all handled with more care than this genre usually gets credit for. Loved every page even the slow ones.
Didn't love it. The internal-monologue-heavy style felt like a barrier between me and the story rather than a way into it.
solid, moving, a bit slow, worth it for the ending alone honestly
Really enjoyed this, altho the middle third definately drags a bit. Thomas and ARIA carry the whole book for me honestly.
Wanted to like this alot more then i did. The writing style just wasnt for me, to much internal monolouge and not enough actually happening on the page.
This book made me cry on public transport which is embarassing but also a genuine compliment. The ending is devastating in the best way.
its okay. some really good moments (the cat reveal especially) but alot of filler inbetween them that couldve been trimmed down.
Couldnt get into it. To slow, to repetative, gave up around chapter 8.

The way she has to figure out structural engineering by trial and error was such a nice touch, felt refreshingly honest compared to most magic systems where the main character conveniently just knows everything.
Decent book, needed a tighter edit imo. There deffinitely some repeated phrasing (she filed it, she catalogued it) that gets noticable after a wile.
loved it!! the thomas stuff got me right in the feels, cant wait for book 2
Ehh. Interesting premise but it never really goes anywhere for most of the book. By the time it picks up its basically over.
One of my favorite reads this year, no question. The grief stuff hit way harder then i expected from a dungeon core book of all things.
This just wasnt for me unfortunatly. The pacing killed it, nothing happens for way to long.
Really solid debut, a little rough around the edges (some repeated sentance structures, a few typos here and there) but the emotional core more then makes up for it.
Fine read. Wouldnt go out of my way to recommend it but wouldnt tell someone to avoid it either. Middle of the road for me.
The trap building sequences got real repetative real fast. Encounter, trigger trap, log data, reset, repeat. Started skimming those parts by the halfway mark.
genuinely didnt expect to care this much about a rock with feelings but here we are. great book
Good ideas, uneven pacing. Worth reading if the premise sounds interesting to you, just dont go in expecting a fast moving plot.
Cant recommend this enough if you like slower, more character driven fantasy. Not for everyone but it was exactly what i wanted.
DNF. way to slow for my taste, and the constant she filed it she catalogued it thing got old real quick
The cat pride subplot snuck up on me, didnt expect to care about Reginald and Trigger as much as i ended up caring. Wish they showed up sooner honestly.
It's alright. Prose is nice but the plot doesnt move much, more of a character study then a story with actual forward momentum.
Wanted more world building and less internal process. We barely learn anything about the actual world this takes place in and then it just ends with a bunch of new questions instead of answers.
such a unique take on the genre, definately not what i was expecting going in but glad i stuck with it
The relationship between ARIA and Thomas is doing something really special that i havent seen done this well before. Quietly devastating the whole way through.
Not for me. To repetative, to slow, and the ending doesnt resolve anything which felt like a cheap way to end book one honestly.
Okay overall. Best parts are clearly the Thomas scenes, everything else felt like it was just there to fill space between them.
Suprisingly emotional for a book about a talking rock building tunnels. The writing style takes some getting used to but its worth it.
The repeated she filed/catalogued/processed thing got real old real fast for me. Good concept buried under a writing tic that shouldve been caught in editing.
not done yet, no rating
Really appreciated that this took the AI consciousness stuff seriously instead of just using it as a gimmick. Smart book, wish more people were talking about it.
It was fine. Didnt blow me away, didnt bore me either. Just kind of sat there in the middle the whole time for me.
Absolutley loved this. The ending wrecked me in the best way. Already counting down for book two.
Not my kind of book. To slow, to abstract, couldnt picture half of what was supposedly happening.
The trap engineering stuff was more interesting then i expected going in. Watching her actually reason through mistakes instead of just powering through them felt refreshing.
Meh. Interesting premise that never really goes anywhere. Kept waiting for the plot to kick into gear and it just never did for me.
Good but flawed. Needs a tighter edit, some repetative sections couldve been cut without losing anything important.
wow. did not expect to get this emotional over a dungeon core book but here we are, thomas and aria absolutely got me
This is the book i didnt know i needed. Smart, sad, unexpectedly funny in places, ending that leaves you desperate for more. Cant wait for book two.
Really didnt work for me. Slow, repetative, and the ending felt like it belonged to a different book entirely.
Decent read overall. The cat mystery subplot was probably my favorite part, wish it got more page time relative to the trap maintenance stuff.
Content warning for anyone picking this up expecting something lighter -- this deals with grief pretty directly and its heavier then the cover suggests. Beautifully done though.
Struggled with this one. The prose kept me at a distance the whole time even in scenes that were clearly supposed to hit emotionally.
3.5 rounding up. Really strong first half, middle third drags a bit, ending brings it back up.
One of the smartest things ive read about grief and identity in any genre, and it happens to be wearing a dungeon core costume while doing it. Highly recommend.
Just couldnt get into the voice. Everything filtered through this real clinical, detatched narration that kept me from ever feeling immersed.
3 stars, solid but unremarkable. Good for a rainy afternoon, wouldnt call it a must read.
